nameStory: The "sticky" in sticky groundsel comes from the plant's glandular hairs that make it feel tacky to the touch, like nature's own sticky tape. The name "groundsel" comes from an old English word meaning "ground swallower," referring to how these plants seem to quickly cover disturbed ground. It's also called "stinking groundsel" because of its unpleasant odor when crushed.
description: Sticky groundsel is a weedy annual plant that belongs to the sunflower family, sporting small yellow daisy-like flowers. This European native typically grows 1-2 feet tall with deeply divided, almost feathery leaves that give it a somewhat ragged appearance. The entire plant has a sticky, glandular coating and produces an unpleasant smell when touched or crushed. While uncommon in New England with only 21 recorded observations, it occasionally pops up in disturbed areas and waste places.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow daisy-like flowers about half an inch across, typically with 8-13 narrow ray petals (the outer "petals") surrounding a yellow center disk, blooming in loose clusters at the top of stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, almost fern-like leaves that are sticky to the touch from tiny glandular hairs; lower leaves are larger and more divided while upper leaves are smaller and less cut

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb growing 1-2 feet tall with branching stems that feel slightly sticky and have a grayish-green color

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant feels distinctly sticky and tacky when touched due to tiny glandular hairs covering stems and leaves

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Produces a strong, unpleasant odor when leaves or stems are crushed or bruised - often described as acrid or fetid

habitat: Look for sticky groundsel in disturbed soils, waste places, roadsides, and areas with poor or sandy soil. As a European introduction, it's most likely to appear in urban and suburban areas where soil has been disturbed. It thrives in sunny, dry locations and is often found near roads, construction sites, or abandoned lots.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic sticky, divided leaves. The sticky texture and unpleasant odor are already noticeable even in young plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time when the small yellow daisy flowers are most abundant, making identification easiest. The sticky coating becomes more pronounced in hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to fluffy white seed heads similar to dandelions. Plants begin to die back but may continue flowering until frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving no above-ground parts. Look for evidence in the form of persistent dried stems in protected areas.

funFact: The sticky coating that gives this plant its name is actually a sophisticated chemical defense system - the glandular hairs produce compounds that can trap small insects and may also help protect the plant from being eaten by larger herbivores who find the texture and smell off-putting.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common groundsel, but sticky groundsel has the distinctive tacky texture and strong odor that common groundsel lacks. Remember: if it's sticky and stinky, it's sticky groundsel!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "groundsel," this plant is not native to New England and is actually considered a weedy introduction from Europe. The Senecio genus contains many species worldwide, some of which are toxic to livestock, though sticky groundsel is rarely abundant enough to cause problems.
compareHints: Sticky groundsel differs from its relative common groundsel by having the distinctive glandular-sticky coating and strong odor that common groundsel lacks. Common groundsel also tends to have less deeply divided leaves and often has flowers without the prominent ray petals, appearing more like small yellow buttons rather than tiny daisies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common groundsel differs from its relative sticky groundsel by being much less sticky to the touch and lacking the strong, unpleasant odor of its cousin.
